newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea ends mourning for Kim Il-sung, hails son.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea ends mourning for Kim Il-sung, hails son.

text.p: North Korea on Tuesday declared an end to a three-year mourning period for "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, but as expected there was no word on when his son Kim Jong-il would take over key state and party posts.
"The mourning is over," announced Foreign Minister Kim Yong-nam at a one-hour ceremony on a vast Pyongyang plaza to honour the founding father of the Stalinist state.
Top figures vowed loyalty to Kim Jong-il as he presided over ceremonies marking the third anniversary of his father's death, indicating he was still firmly in control.

Dressed in a high-collared black tunic, he stood expressionless and silently on a podium in front of the former Kumsusan presidential palace, now a memorial hall where his father's embalmed body lies.
Tens of thousands of soldiers and ranks of grey-suited officials stood to attention as a 16-gun salute rang out.
North Korea watchers said the end of mourning sets the stage for Kim Jong-il to assume the titles of state president and general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party.
But while Pyongyang has hinted at a formal power transfer following the traditional mourning, analysts said they believed Kim Jong-il would wait several more months.

To act too quickly might seem unfilial. Besides, Kim Jong-il might be loathe to step completely into his father's shoes while the nation's economy is in ruins and the population is on the brink of famine, the analysts say.
State media used Kim Jong-il's formal military titles during the ceremony.
"We solemnly re-state our heartful pledge to our father, the Great Leader, at this important occassion when the mourning is over," Kim Yong-nam said.

"All party members, officers and men of the People's Army and the people will always believe in and follow only comrade Kim Jong-il in any circumstances," he said after the crowd observed a brief silence.
Kim Jong-il, 55, appeared healthy as he listened to representatives of the Workers' Party, government and military hailing him as leader. He did not make a speech.
Kim Jong-il has been groomed for decades to take over in the communist world's first dynastic succession.

Vice-Marshal Jo Myong-rok, widely tipped to fill the vacant post of defence minister, said the military would "rally close around comrade Kim Jong-il in one mind and accomplish by force of arms the cause of the president left unfinished".
The support of the 1.1 million-strong military is vital for Kim Jong-il, who lacks the charisma of his father and faces the task of rescuing the economy.
Pictures broadcast by Pyongyang state television showed no signs of the hunger that stalks the country.

A well-dressed crowd faced a colossal granite palace against a backdrop of skyscrapers decorated with red banners reading "Defend the headquarters of the revolution headed by the great comrade Kim Jong-il with our lives" and "We honour the memory of the Great Leader, comrade Kim Il-sung".
A giant portrait of Kim Il-sung hung on the wall of the palace. A full military brass band played solemn music.

Some North Korea watchers in Seoul and Tokyo said Kim Jong-il was expected to take up the two leadership posts later this year, probably around the October 10 anniversary of the founding of the Workers' Party.

"By insisting on a traditional three-year mourning period, the North has tried to earn time to put its economic troubles behind it before anointing Kim Jong-il," said Lee Ki-won of the Institute of North Korea Studies in Seoul.
"It now has no other excuse.
"Pyongyang will have to call the party's central committee to elect its general secretary or let various social groups stage rallies pleading with Kim Jong-il to assume the presidency," he said.
